That's a good question. I imagine you can block specific IP addresses, or a range of addresses.

You can also edit your operating system host file to exclude identified addresses, or add those addresses to your firewall block list.

You can also block specific sites using your adblock anti spam software within your browsers.

Any of these would prevent your browser from accessing these addresses. However, when websites send to these addresses, the browser will sometimes appear to stall, waiting for replies that cannot be returned. This can cause some pages to take a very long time to load, because you have to wait for the timeout before loading the rest of the site will proceed. A small price to pay for improved privacy.

I use the full range of protection - firewall, antivirus, multiple anti spam browser add ons. This includes cache clearing and cookie removals between sessions, and various spoofing technologies to confuse trackers. Partly this is to promote privacy, partly this is to promote security, especially against viruses, and partly to improve website appearance, so as sites are not gummed up with advertising overkill.

I also use an alternative browser. Mainstream browsers are problematic now concerning privacy.

In spite of all of that, I still find it necessary to individually block various page elements from time to time.

I'm not trying to block all advertising. In fact I do not do so. It's the intrusive advertising and pop ups are my main concern.

I find the anti tracking add ons, Ghostery, Decentraleyes, uBlock Origin, Privacy Badger, Better Privacy, and Adblock Plus, in combination, effectively block 99.999% of all known, and some unknown, tracking activity. You can also use browser ID spoofing to send false data to trackers, though this can be quite a bit more complicated.

I consider this to be a basic level of consumer protection. Not the sort of protection that provides genuine privacy, but enough to protect you from most of the commercial abuse web users encounter in their daily travels.
